page.layout: One page of text, single column; Greek and English verse set as indented lines; footnotes in small type at the foot in two columns (left: letters o, q, r; right: letter p).

main_text.p: saith Pindarus. "The man that doth things befitting him, forgetteth hades:" meaning, that the remembrance of death doth no whit trouble him. And again:
"The son of Cleonicus wisheth that with such manners he may meet and receive hades," that is, death, "and hoar old age." The like hath Euripides in his Alcestis:
main_text.l: Σκοτία δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ὄσσοισιν νὺξ ἐφέρπει.
And darksome night doth creep upon mine eyes.
main_text.p: And another poet, cited by Plutarchq :
main_text.l: Λιμὴν γὰρ ὄντως ἀίδας ἀν᾽ αἶαν.
main_text.p: "O death, the sovereign physician, come: for hades is in very truth the haven of the earth." So the saying, "That the best thing were, never to have been born, and the next to this, to die quickly;" is thus expressed by Theognis, in his elegies:
main_text.l: Πάντων᾽ μὲν μὴ φῦναι ἐπιχθονίοισιν ἄριστον,
Φύντα δ᾽ ὅπως ὤκιστα πύλας ἀίδαο περῆσαι,
main_text.p: q Plutarch. de Consolat. ad Apollon.

page.notes: Footnote letters o, q, r, p are reference marks in the Greek and English text; the reference marks in the text are printed as superscript letters and are not further marked. The Greek verse lines are reproduced as printed; the first line of the Pindar epigraph and the dash-led lines are as printed. Line "Τοίαισιν ὀργαῖς" and "᾿Αντιάσας" have an ambiguous breathing/accent in the scan. The lines "Ω θάνατε" and "Λιμὴν" are fairly clear but some accents are uncertain.
